body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students use economic indicators (unemployment, output, bank failures, stock prices) to describe the Depression and evaluate the New Deal's effects (D2.Eco.11.9-12, RH.9-10.7).
- Students analyze how Roosevelt redefined freedom and the federal government's responsibilities in 1933 and 1941 (D2.His.1.9-12, D2.Civ.6.9-12, RH.9-10.2).
- Students evaluate Executive Order 9066 and the 1988 Civil Liberties Act, and how the perspectives of 1942 and 1988 differ (D2.His.5.9-12, D2.His.11.9-12, D2.Civ.14.9-12).
- Students argue whether the New Deal ended the Great Depression, weighing monetary and fiscal policy choices (D2.Eco.12.9-12, D2.His.16.9-12, D4.1.9-12).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: The Great Depression in Numbers, Roosevelt's first inaugural, the Four Freedoms, Executive Order 9066, the Civil Liberties Act of 1988
- Graph paper or a spreadsheet for the unemployment line graph
- Optional: public-domain Farm Security Administration photographs (for example, Dorothea Lange's work for the federal government); public-domain War Relocation Authority photographs of the camps
- A note on language: the federal government called the camps "relocation centers" and the policy "evacuation." Many historians and the Japanese American community now use "incarceration" and "forced removal." Discuss the choice of words with students (D2.His.7).

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Fear Itself. Lesson activity: Reading the Depression in Numbers. Students graph unemployment from 1929 to 1944 and annotate it with key events.
Day 2: Debrief the graph: what happened in 1937-1938, and why does unemployment fall fastest after 1941? Introduce relief, recovery and reform. Begin Fear Itself and Four Freedoms.
Day 3: Finish Fear Itself and Four Freedoms. Connect the Four Freedoms to Pearl Harbor and the war effort.
Day 4: A Grave Injustice: read Executive Order 9066 and the 1988 findings side by side; link to the free speech cases of 1918-1919. Students write the analysis.
Day 5: Unit assessment: Did the New Deal End the Depression? (no AI help; students may use the data reading and their graphs).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a pre-labeled graph with axes and the first three years plotted. Pair students to read the data aloud before graphing.
- Support: give a two-column organizer for EO 9066 and the 1988 act: What the government said, What it did, Why (according to the source).
- Extension: research Korematsu v. United States (1944) and Trump v. Hawaii (2018), in which the Court said Korematsu "was gravely wrong the day it was decided," and explain how judgments of the past change.
- Extension: compare unemployment in the Great Depression and the Great Recession (2008-2010) using current federal data.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): pre-teach economic vocabulary with the graph itself (point to rising and falling lines). Offer frames: "Unemployment rose from ___ percent in ___ to ___ percent in ___." Allow oral rehearsal of the claim with a partner before writing.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are studying the Great Depression and the Second World War. Students are reading unemployment data, Franklin Roosevelt's speeches, and the government's 1988 apology for imprisoning Japanese Americans during the war. If your family has stories from the 1930s or 1940s, or of any hard economic time, this is a wonderful unit to share them. Ask your student: what should the government do when one worker in four has no job?
title: Teacher guide: Depression and the Second World War
